Summary
Pediatric rehabilitation for chronic ankle instability (CAI) and acute lateral ankle sprains (LAS) shares foundational elements (protection, restoration of ROM, strength, and balance), but diverges in emphasis, timing, and intensity. Acute LAS protocols prioritize early protected loading, pain and swelling control, and phased return-to-sport with sport-specific drills; CAI protocols add long-term neuromuscular retraining to address proprioceptive loss, altered motor control, and recurrent instability risk. <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Modern lateral ankle sprain rehabilitation integrates graded neuromuscular and proprioceptive exercises beyond RICE, with more aggressive programs for athletes at high recurrence risk</cite> <cite id="40f2ed36-4">Adolescents with CAI commonly show impaired neuro-motor control, proprioception deficits, altered proximal/distal activation patterns, reduced peroneus longus cross-sectional area, and a higher risk of giving-way symptoms</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Balance and proprioceptive-based programs improve postural control and reduce instability symptoms in pediatric CAI</cite>.

1) Time course and goals
- Acute LAS: Goals in the first days to weeks are pain control, swelling reduction, early protected mobilization, and restoration of basic ROM and balance, progressing to sport-specific drills. <cite id="40f2ed36-0">RICE remains a baseline, but early phased functional support with supervised exercise and graded proprioceptive and neuromuscular training is recommended, especially for athletes</cite> <cite id="92a03876-2">Pediatric eligibility and inclusion typically cover acute LAS within 7 days, with baseline and discharge standardized measures to guide progression</cite>.
- CAI: Goals are multi-pronged—restore structural integrity where present, but primarily retrain sensorimotor control, proprioception, and joint stability to reduce recurrence. <cite id="7091dbdb-2">Conservative CAI care combines strength, proprioceptive, ROM, and manual therapy; dynamic neuromuscular stabilization and vestibular/balance training are emphasized to restore control and reduce reinjury risk</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-0">Neuromuscular control training is a protective strategy for the previously injured ankle and can reduce subsequent lower-limb injuries</cite>.

2) Pediatric acute LAS rehabilitation specifics
- Initial management and loading: <cite id="92a03876-1">Early joint mobilization in pediatrics is supported by RCTs in acute LAS, addressing the safety and efficacy beyond adult extrapolations; pediatric protocols can incorporate traction-assisted mobilization with attention to return-to-sport time</cite>. <cite id="92a03876-3">For severe (grade III) pediatric ankle sprains, aquatic therapy in early rehabilitation is being tested to shorten back-to-sport time while maintaining proprioceptive and balance outcomes versus land-based rehab</cite>.
- Strengthening and functional progression: <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Aggressive but graded neuromuscular and proprioceptive exercises are used to facilitate early recovery and address instability risk</cite>. <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Resistance training typically targets lateral ankle musculature (peroneals), improves inversion/eversion strength, and is complemented by balance training to enhance rapid joint positioning in dynamic sports; plyometrics can improve strength and function in athletes within 4–6 weeks</cite>.
- Pediatric-specific considerations: <cite id="92a03876-2">Eligibility and trial designs often restrict to 8–18 years with acute (<3–7 days) lateral sprains, exclude syndesmotic injuries, and emphasize caregiver involvement and adherence to follow-up</cite>. <cite id="92a03876-1">Pediatric protocols may shorten immobilization and emphasize early, monitored mobilization to allow functional recovery with careful return-to-sport timing</cite>.

3) Pediatric CAI rehabilitation specifics
- Assessment and individualized planning: <cite id="7091dbdb-1">In children with CAI, ankle joint repositioning accuracy shows learning and fatigue effects; brief, reliable testing protocols (3 trials overall, or 4 for inversion, 5 for eversion) are recommended to guide progression and avoid overfatigue during reassessments</cite>.
- Core deficits and targeted retraining: <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Pediatric CAI commonly presents with functional “giving way,” mechanical instability with ligamentous/pericapsular laxity, muscle weakness, and proprioceptor damage; neuromotor impairment and sensory reorganization contribute to impaired postural control</cite>. <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Eccentric eversion strengthening can improve ankle score and functional tests when compared to balance-only programs, while balance training reduces reinjury risk in young athletes</cite>.
- Modalities and technology: <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Virtual reality–based balance training has been compared with conventional Biodex balance in adolescents with CAI, with evidence that balance programs improve postural control and that multiple modalities can enhance engagement and outcomes</cite>.
- Graded neuromuscular stabilization: <cite id="7091dbdb-2">Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization approaches are advocated to address sensorimotor and arthrokinematic impairments alongside conventional strength and proprioceptive exercises, aiming to reduce recurrence and optimize long-term outcomes</cite>.
- Family/athlete education and compliance: <cite id="7091dbdb-2">External psychological support and adherence strategies are integral, given underdiagnosis and high recurrence rates even in youth</cite>.

4) Key distinguishing elements
- Emphasis and sequencing:
  - Acute LAS: early, monitored loading and pain control; then progressive ROM, balance, and sport-specific drills. <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Early functional support and graded neuromuscular/proprioceptive exercises are emphasized to prevent chronicity</cite> <cite id="92a03876-3">Aquatic early rehab can accelerate sports return while preserving proprioception in severe cases</cite>.
  - CAI: longer-term, high-intensity neuromuscular retraining to normalize joint position sense, motor control, and muscle timing; continued eccentric strengthening of inverters/peroneals. <cite id="7091dbdb-1">Proprioceptive deficits in CAI justify dedicated balance programs with brief, reliable testing to individualize progression</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Neuromotor impairment and altered activation patterns necessitate multi-component programs beyond isolated ligament strengthening</cite>.
- Muscle and joint focus:
  - Acute LAS: restore everters/inverters symmetry, peroneal function, and joint mechanics; add plyometrics as tolerated. <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Resistance and balance training improve strength and neuromuscular control; peroneal strengthening is central; plyometrics improve strength and function within 4–6 weeks</cite>.
  - CAI: target sensory reorganization and central control strategies, often using complex perturbation-based balance/vestibular training; address accessory motion and “neutral zone” enlargement. <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Proprioceptive damage, enlarged neutral zone, and altered proximal–distal activation are common, improved by tailored balance programs</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-2">Balance/vestibular training enhances proprioception and neuromuscular control to reduce reinjury risk</cite>.
- Return-to-sport criteria:
  - Acute LAS: pain-free ROM and strength, functional hop tests, sport-specific agility, and a gradual return with sport- and level-dependent milestones. <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Phased programs with supervised exercise and functional support guide early recovery and return to sport</cite> <cite id="92a03876-1">Early mobilization RCTs in pediatric LAS examine return-to-sport times and functional outcomes</cite>.
  - CAI: stability without subjective giving way, normalized joint position sense, adequate dynamic balance and single-leg hop, and successful functional testing under fatigue; gradual return with neuromuscular drills integrated. <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Ankle score and hop tests respond to balance and resistance training, supporting sport return when functional thresholds are met</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Adolescents with CAI benefit from programs that close deficits in postural control and neuromotor function before resuming sports</cite>.
- Adjuncts and progression:
  - Pediatric LAS: taping for early protection or pain modulation; bracing in high-risk athletes; early aquatic therapy for severe cases; non-restraint strategies may be compared to foster compliance and functional recovery. <cite id="92a03876-3">Aquatic therapy is proposed to facilitate early return with preserved balance and power in grade III sprains</cite>.
  - Pediatric CAI: progressive bracing/taping during sport; neuromuscular taping or braces as psychological and mechanical supports; step-down from braces as control improves; consider tenodesis/repair in persistent mechanical instability or recurrent symptoms despite rehab. <cite id="40f2ed36-3">Arthroscopic repair for complex ankle sprains with early rehabilitation is an option when conservative care fails, with potential advantages over older open techniques</cite>.

5) Return-to-sport and surgical thresholds in pediatrics
- Nonoperative pathways: <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Aggressive, phased rehab with supervised exercise and proprioceptive training is preferred to restore function and reduce recurrence risk</cite>. <cite id="92a03876-1">Pediatric early mobilization trials assess return-to-sport timelines; traction-assisted mobilization aims to reduce time lost while maintaining function</cite>.
- Referral to surgery: <cite id="40f2ed36-3">When instability persists despite adequate conservative care or in complex proximal ligament injuries, surgical repair with structured early rehabilitation can enable earlier sport return with fewer complications compared to older cast-immobilization protocols</cite>. <cite id="7091dbdb-2">The International Ankle Consortium promotes evidence-informed protocols addressing sensorimotor and arthrokinematic impairments to lower recurrence; surgery is reserved for refractory cases</cite>.

6) Pediatric-specific risk factors and compliance strategies
- Risk profiles: <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Males have higher incidence of mild CAI than females in adolescents; history of prior AS increases susceptibility to CAI</cite>. <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Structural deformity and inadequate rehabilitation increase CAI risk; recurrence rates for ankle sprains are 12–47% and athletes with prior AS have ~3.5× higher injury rate</cite>.
- Biomechanical and training adaptations: <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Peroneus longus cross-sectional area reductions have been observed after lateral AS, indicating muscular adaptations</cite>. <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Plyometric and resistance training can correct deficits in strength and function within short windows, supporting pediatric athletes’ readiness for sport</cite>.
- Assessment efficiency: <cite id="7091dbdb-1">In pediatric CAI, 3-trial joint repositioning protocols (or 4 inversion, 5 eversion) are reliable and mitigate learning/fatigue effects, improving adherence to frequent progressions</cite>.
- Care model: <cite id="7091dbdb-2">Pediatric CAI often requires integrated psychological support and adherence strategies due to underdiagnosis and high recurrence even in young populations</cite>. <cite id="92a03876-2">Protocols commonly include caregiver involvement, clear inclusion/exclusion (no syndesmotic injury), and structured discharge criteria</cite>.

Practical distinctions at a glance
- Acute pediatric LAS: prioritize early, monitored mobilization and pain control; add graded balance, peroneal strengthening, and sport-specific drills; consider aquatic therapy for severe sprains and non-restraint strategies to improve compliance. <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Early functional support and supervised, graded neuromuscular/proprioceptive training are central</cite> <cite id="92a03876-1">Pediatric early mobilization RCTs guide return-to-sport time and safety</cite> <cite id="92a03876-3">Aquatic rehab can decrease recovery time while preserving balance and power in grade III injuries</cite>.
- Pediatric CAI: emphasize long-term neuromuscular retraining to normalize joint position sense, postural control, and muscle timing; integrate eccentric inversion/eversion strengthening, balance/vestibular training, and progressive bracing/taping; consider tenodesis/repair for persistent mechanical instability; personalize with sex-specific risk and biomechanical factors. <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Neuromotor and proprioceptive deficits are core targets in adolescents with CAI</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Eccentric eversion strengthening and balance programs improve functional scores and reduce reinjury risk</cite> <cite id="40f2ed36-3">Surgical options with early rehab provide structured pathways when conservative care fails</cite>.

Bottom line
For pediatric patients, acute LAS protocols are time-limited, load-controlled, and functionally progressive, while pediatric CAI protocols are prolonged, neuromuscularly focused, and centred on restoring proprioception, motor control, and stability to prevent recurrence; both benefit from supervised progression, parent involvement, and selective use of bracing or aquatic therapy, with surgery reserved for refractory mechanical instability. <cite id="40f2ed36-0">Early phased rehab with graded neuromuscular/proprioceptive exercises reduces chronicity risk</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-3">Adolescent CAI requires proprioceptive and neuromuscular retraining due to persistent deficits</cite> <cite id="92a03876-1">Pediatric acute protocols increasingly incorporate early mobilization and structured return-to-sport assessments</cite> <cite id="7091dbdb-4">Strength and balance programs measurably improve function and reduce reinjury risk in youth</cite>.

Title: How Many Trials are Needed to Assess Ankle Joint Proprioception in Children with Chronic Ankle Instability?
Snippet: The assessment of ankle joint repositioning is commonly used to detect joint impairment in people with chronic ankle instability (CAI). To decrease measurement fluctuation errors, it has been suggested that an average of 10 measurements be utilized. However, learning and tiredness difficulties, particularly in children, might make this difficult. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the repeatability of 3 and 10 measures of ankle joint repositioning using an isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex) in children with CAI. Ten children with CAI with an average age of 11.21 years were recruited in the study. The ankle inversion and eversion angles for 3 and 10 trials using active and passive reproduction protocols were recorded using Biodex Multi-Joint System 4TM.  The error of reproduction angle was presented by the mean, correlation, and percentage changes for both active and passive reposition angles. The means of the error for ankle joint reproduction angles revealed no significant differences between 3 and 10 trials for both active and passive protocols (p > 0.05). The ICC(3,1) revealed high correlations between 3 and 10 trials of assessments (ICC(3,1) = 0.82 - 0.91). The percentage changes of means and standard deviations showed learning effect of ankle joint proprioception measurement after the 4th and the 5th trials for inversion and eversion, respectively. Therefore, to prevent learning and fatigue effects, a 3-trial protocol would be more appropriate than a 10-trial protocol. However, a 4-trial protocol and a 5-trial protocol were suggested for inversion and eversion, respectively. The suggested protocols are recommended to use for further reliability studies of the ankle joint proprioception in children with CAI. 
HIGHLIGHTS

Ankle joint reproduction assessments using active and passive protocols are needed to identify the impairment of joint position sense in children with chronic ankle instability
To prevent fatigue effect, 3 trials are sufficient for testing of ankle joint position sense in children with chronic ankle instability
In research setting, a 4-trial protocol for ankle joint inversion and a 5-trial protocol for ankle joint eversion are more appropriate than a 10-trial protocol

Title: Dynamic neuromuscular stabilization, balance, and conventional training for chronic ankle instability in amateur athletes: a randomised controlled trial
Snippet: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) results from recurrent lateral ankle sprains, causing persistent pain, instability, sensations of the ankle "giving way", structural changes, and adaptations in the sensorimotor and vestibular systems. It represents a significant global musculoskeletal health concern with implications that extend far beyond the athletic population [1][2][3]. The long-term consequences of CAI include not only sensorimotor and vestibular system dysfunction, but also early-onset posttraumatic osteoarthritis of the ankle, reduced physical activity levels, and decreased quality of life, even in young individuals [4,5]. Epidemiological data indicate that the prevalence of CAI varies by age and activity level, with rates up to 29% among high school students, 23.4% in high school and college athletes and 20% in adolescent athletes [6][7][8]. Importantly, this condition is frequently underdiagnosed or misperceived as benign, leading to insufficient rehabilitation and high recurrence rates [6,9]. 

Ankle deformity recovery, particularly in cases of CAI, requires a multifaceted approach that integrates conservative treatments, including physical therapy, external support, and psychological support [10,11]. Physical therapy interventions commonly integrate strength exercises, proprioceptive training, and range-of-motion exercises with manual therapy techniques [3,10,12,13]. However, conventional training methods may not fully address the dynamic and complex nature of ankle instability, and may not sufficiently restore neuromuscular control or prevent recurrence of instability. Therefore, the International Ankle Consortium advocates for evidence-informed rehabilitation protocols that address both sensorimotor and arthrokinematic impairments, to reduce recurrence risk and optimize long-term outcomes [5,14,15]. 

Balance and vestibular training has been shown to enhance proprioception, postural stability, and neuromuscular control factors that are vital for restoring ankle function and reducing the risk of reinjury in individuals with CAI [16,17]. However, one emerging approach that may offer even broader benefits is Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization (DNS).

Modern methods of rehabilitation are more aggressive; in addition to the rest, ice, compression, and elevation (RICE) protocols, early phased functional support and supervised exercise therapy are considered better for early recovery. This should include graded neuromuscular and proprioceptive exercises over during the recovery phase. Specialized ankle stability programs need to be considered for professional athletes, with special attention to individual risk factors that could predispose them to recurrent lateral ankle sprains. The management protocol for recurrent sprains, although similar, needs to be more aggressive depending on the extent of the injury, duration since the first injury, and the associated instability. Modern methods include computerized documentation and the use of robots to oversee rehabilitation protocols.

Title: How Many Trials are Needed to Assess Ankle Joint Proprioception in Children with Chronic Ankle Instability?
Snippet: The assessment of ankle joint repositioning is commonly used to detect joint impairment in people with chronic ankle instability (CAI). To decrease measurement fluctuation errors, it has been suggested that an average of 10 measurements be utilized. However, learning and tiredness difficulties, particularly in children, might make this difficult. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the repeatability of 3 and 10 measures of ankle joint repositioning using an isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex) in children with CAI. Ten children with CAI with an average age of 11.21 years were recruited in the study. The ankle inversion and eversion angles for 3 and 10 trials using active and passive reproduction protocols were recorded using Biodex Multi-Joint System 4TM.  The error of reproduction angle was presented by the mean, correlation, and percentage changes for both active and passive reposition angles. The means of the error for ankle joint reproduction angles revealed no significant differences between 3 and 10 trials for both active and passive protocols (p > 0.05). The ICC(3,1) revealed high correlations between 3 and 10 trials of assessments (ICC(3,1) = 0.82 - 0.91). The percentage changes of means and standard deviations showed learning effect of ankle joint proprioception measurement after the 4th and the 5th trials for inversion and eversion, respectively. Therefore, to prevent learning and fatigue effects, a 3-trial protocol would be more appropriate than a 10-trial protocol. However, a 4-trial protocol and a 5-trial protocol were suggested for inversion and eversion, respectively. The suggested protocols are recommended to use for further reliability studies of the ankle joint proprioception in children with CAI. 
HIGHLIGHTS

Ankle joint reproduction assessments using active and passive protocols are needed to identify the impairment of joint position sense in children with chronic ankle instability
To prevent fatigue effect, 3 trials are sufficient for testing of ankle joint position sense in children with chronic ankle instability
In research setting, a 4-trial protocol for ankle joint inversion and a 5-trial protocol for ankle joint eversion are more appropriate than a 10-trial protocol

Title: Dynamic neuromuscular stabilization, balance, and conventional training for chronic ankle instability in amateur athletes: a randomised controlled trial
Snippet: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) results from recurrent lateral ankle sprains, causing persistent pain, instability, sensations of the ankle "giving way", structural changes, and adaptations in the sensorimotor and vestibular systems. It represents a significant global musculoskeletal health concern with implications that extend far beyond the athletic population [1][2][3]. The long-term consequences of CAI include not only sensorimotor and vestibular system dysfunction, but also early-onset posttraumatic osteoarthritis of the ankle, reduced physical activity levels, and decreased quality of life, even in young individuals [4,5]. Epidemiological data indicate that the prevalence of CAI varies by age and activity level, with rates up to 29% among high school students, 23.4% in high school and college athletes and 20% in adolescent athletes [6][7][8]. Importantly, this condition is frequently underdiagnosed or misperceived as benign, leading to insufficient rehabilitation and high recurrence rates [6,9]. 

Ankle deformity recovery, particularly in cases of CAI, requires a multifaceted approach that integrates conservative treatments, including physical therapy, external support, and psychological support [10,11]. Physical therapy interventions commonly integrate strength exercises, proprioceptive training, and range-of-motion exercises with manual therapy techniques [3,10,12,13]. However, conventional training methods may not fully address the dynamic and complex nature of ankle instability, and may not sufficiently restore neuromuscular control or prevent recurrence of instability. Therefore, the International Ankle Consortium advocates for evidence-informed rehabilitation protocols that address both sensorimotor and arthrokinematic impairments, to reduce recurrence risk and optimize long-term outcomes [5,14,15]. 

Balance and vestibular training has been shown to enhance proprioception, postural stability, and neuromuscular control factors that are vital for restoring ankle function and reducing the risk of reinjury in individuals with CAI [16,17]. However, one emerging approach that may offer even broader benefits is Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization (DNS).

Snippet: Ankle sprain occurs mainly on the lateral side due to inversion of the ankle, and is a common sports injury with a high recurrence rate [1]. CAI occurs in 40-70% of individuals with repetitive ankle sprains, and factors contributing to the development of CAI include the severity of the injury, structural deformity, and inadequate rehabilitation [4,5].

documents.title: How Many Trials are Needed to Assess Ankle Joint Proprioception in Children with Chronic Ankle Instability?
documents.snippet:
The assessment of ankle joint repositioning is commonly used to detect joint impairment in people with chronic ankle instability (CAI). To decrease measurement fluctuation errors, it has been suggested that an average of 10 measurements be utilized. However, learning and tiredness difficulties, particularly in children, might make this difficult. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the repeatability of 3 and 10 measures of ankle joint repositioning using an isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex) in children with CAI. Ten children with CAI with an average age of 11.21 years were recruited in the study. The ankle inversion and eversion angles for 3 and 10 trials using active and passive reproduction protocols were recorded using Biodex Multi-Joint System 4TM.  The error of reproduction angle was presented by the mean, correlation, and percentage changes for both active and passive reposition angles. The means of the error for ankle joint reproduction angles revealed no significant differences between 3 and 10 trials for both active and passive protocols (p > 0.05). The ICC(3,1) revealed high correlations between 3 and 10 trials of assessments (ICC(3,1) = 0.82 - 0.91). The percentage changes of means and standard deviations showed learning effect of ankle joint proprioception measurement after the 4th and the 5th trials for inversion and eversion, respectively. Therefore, to prevent learning and fatigue effects, a 3-trial protocol would be more appropriate than a 10-trial protocol. However, a 4-trial protocol and a 5-trial protocol were suggested for inversion and eversion, respectively. The suggested protocols are recommended to use for further reliability studies of the ankle joint proprioception in children with CAI. 
HIGHLIGHTS

Ankle joint reproduction assessments using active and passive protocols are needed to identify the impairment of joint position sense in children with chronic ankle instability
To prevent fatigue effect, 3 trials are sufficient for testing of ankle joint position sense in children with chronic ankle instability
In research setting, a 4-trial protocol for ankle joint inversion and a 5-trial protocol for ankle joint eversion are more appropriate than a 10-trial protocol

Chronic ankle instability (CAI) results from recurrent lateral ankle sprains, causing persistent pain, instability, sensations of the ankle "giving way", structural changes, and adaptations in the sensorimotor and vestibular systems. It represents a significant global musculoskeletal health concern with implications that extend far beyond the athletic population [1][2][3]. The long-term consequences of CAI include not only sensorimotor and vestibular system dysfunction, but also early-onset posttraumatic osteoarthritis of the ankle, reduced physical activity levels, and decreased quality of life, even in young individuals [4,5]. Epidemiological data indicate that the prevalence of CAI varies by age and activity level, with rates up to 29% among high school students, 23.4% in high school and college athletes and 20% in adolescent athletes [6][7][8]. Importantly, this condition is frequently underdiagnosed or misperceived as benign, leading to insufficient rehabilitation and high recurrence rates [6,9]. 

Ankle deformity recovery, particularly in cases of CAI, requires a multifaceted approach that integrates conservative treatments, including physical therapy, external support, and psychological support [10,11]. Physical therapy interventions commonly integrate strength exercises, proprioceptive training, and range-of-motion exercises with manual therapy techniques [3,10,12,13]. However, conventional training methods may not fully address the dynamic and complex nature of ankle instability, and may not sufficiently restore neuromuscular control or prevent recurrence of instability. Therefore, the International Ankle Consortium advocates for evidence-informed rehabilitation protocols that address both sensorimotor and arthrokinematic impairments, to reduce recurrence risk and optimize long-term outcomes [5,14,15]. 

Balance and vestibular training has been shown to enhance proprioception, postural stability, and neuromuscular control factors that are vital for restoring ankle function and reducing the risk of reinjury in individuals with CAI [16,17]. However, one emerging approach that may offer even broader benefits is Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization (DNS).

Summary of the issue
Pediatric lateral ankle instability carries unique risks because open growth plates and skeletal immaturity alter ligamentous restraint, joint biomechanics, and bone remodeling responses to stress. Rehabilitation must therefore emphasize physeal protection, neuromuscular and proprioceptive stabilization, activity modification to avoid high-risk cutting/landing, and careful timing of sport return, with surgery tailored to preserve growth when indicated. The overarching principle is to restore functional stability while minimizing valgus-inversion overload and ensuring the physis remains unimpeded through appropriate bracing, progressive loading, and, when persistent, physeal-sparing ligament or bone procedures. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Pediatric lateral ligament reconstruction can achieve good outcomes when surgeons respect physeal anatomy and allow faster rehabilitation and return to preinjury activity</cite> and <cite id="3443e106-1">functional bracing with early mobilization is more effective than immobilization for pediatric ankle sprains, with bracing recommended 3–6 months postreturn to activity and indefinitely for persistent instability, alongside balance and proprioception training</cite>.

Principles specific to open growth plates and skeletal immaturity
- Protect the physeal mechanism: Loading and rehabilitation should avoid physeal arrest or distraction. Surgical options in children must preserve the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and distal tibial physeal blood supply; modified Broström-Gould techniques with physeal-sparing are favored and allow accelerated rehab when used for persistent instability after failed conservative care. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Modified Broström-Gould with internal bracing in pediatric chronic lateral instability improved pain and function and enabled return to sport, contingent on respecting growth plate anatomy</cite>. 
- Emphasize neuromuscular and proprioceptive control: Pediatric programs should prioritize balance, coordination, and cut-down control due to higher recurrence risk and developmental instability perception. <cite id="3443e106-1">Chronic instability rehabilitation in pediatrics stresses continued physiotherapy with balance and proprioception</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-1">pediatric growth plate injury with concomitant ligament strain requires tailored rehab including neuromuscular and proprioceptive training to restore stability and facilitate safe return</cite>.
- Modify high-risk activities during open physis: Instability and immature joint orientation increase valgus-inversion risk during multidirectional jump-landing and cutting, elevating recurrence risk and stressing ATFL/CFL. Early sport return in non-matured ankles should be cautious to avoid cutting/landing until biomechanics and strength are reestablished. <cite id="018126a8-0">Athletes with chronic ankle instability show higher recurrent-sprain risk during lateral and diagonal landings vs forward jumps, underscoring the need for more effective rehab to prevent recurrence</cite> and <cite id="e5e9a520-0">forefoot vs rearfoot landing strategies shift knee vs ankle risk factors, with forefoot increasing ankle inversion/inversion moment, highlighting the need to teach safer footstrike and cutting mechanics</cite>.

Conservative care: sequencing, bracing, and return-to-play
- Initial management and progression: PRICE early, then progressive weightbearing, range of motion, and strengthening with emphasis on functional control. Bracing or taping can enhance perceived stability but may not improve objective performance, so programs should not rely solely on supports; they should facilitate earlier mobilization with gradual return. <cite id="3443e106-1">Functional bracing with early mobilization outperforms immobilization for pediatric sprains, and bracing is recommended 3–6 months after return to activity and indefinitely with chronic instability, alongside proprioceptive training</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-3">functional braces that restrict external rotation (e.g., Malleoloc) are used after brief immobilization/casting and CAM booting, with serial radiographs to confirm mortise alignment and a tailored return-to-play protocol</cite>. 
- Bracing vs objective function: Supports mainly improve self-reported function and psychological readiness rather than gross functional tests; thus, they should be used as an adjunct while rehab restores control and strength. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-4">Taping or bracing significantly improved Ankle-GO self-reported scores and perceived stability but did not change objective functional tests in adults with CAI</cite>. This pattern supports using braces conservatively in pediatrics to reduce recurrence perception while prioritizing neuromuscular and proprioceptive gains.
- Osteochondral protection in adolescents: High activity levels in juveniles increase microtrauma risk to the talus; rehab should include joint-protective loading, sport cessation during symptomatic spikes, and monitoring for osteochondral lesions. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-2">Adolescents frequently participate in organized sports, exposing ankles to repetitive microtrauma with relatively high incidence of juvenile osteochondral lesions; pediatric management aims to optimize outcomes across modalities</cite>.
- Treatment variability and the need for individualized plans: Pediatric lateral ankle injury management varies widely among clinicians, with inconsistent rationale between ankle vs syndesmotic injuries and between open vs closed physeas. This underscores the need for careful assessment and shared decision-making on immobilization duration, bracing, and referral to physical therapy. <cite id="3443e106-3">Surveyed pediatric orthopaedic practice shows variability in management of adult vs syndesmotic injuries in children, underrepresentation of low-energy lateral injuries in the literature, and that immobilization and therapy practices differ with limited evidence-based consensus</cite>.

Activity modification and return-to-sport in open physis
- Avoid high-valgus-inversion tasks initially: Restrict noncontact cutting, change-of-direction drills, and multidirectional jump-landing until ankle inversion range and knee valgus control normalize, and proprioception and strength are sport-specific. Teach toe-out/forefoot strike caution due to trade-offs in knee vs ankle risk. <cite id="018126a8-0">Lateral and diagonal landings pose greater recurrence risk than forward jumps for CAI athletes, implying targeted avoidance and retraining of these tasks</cite> and <cite id="e5e9a520-0">forefoot strategies can reduce knee valgus but may increase ankle inversion/inversion moment, so individualized technique training is required</cite>.

- Duration of support and sport restrictions: Continue lace-up bracing or functional taping during high-risk sports or drills for 3–6 months postreturn to activity, and indefinitely if chronic instability persists; avoid bracing as a sole strategy and combine with control and strengthening. <cite id="3443e106-1">Bracing for 3–6 months after return to activity and indefinitely in persistent instability is recommended, with continued physiotherapy</cite>.
- Psychological readiness vs objective control: Because supports improve perceived stability without necessarily improving objective tests, integrate sport-specific drills that restore dynamic balance and coordination before full return, using perceived instability and drill performance as decision points. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-4">Ankle supports enhance self-reported and perceived stability but not objective functional test performance, so objective control should drive return decisions</cite>.

- Indications and timing: Failed pediatric conservative care with persistent mechanical instability (positive drawer/translation), pain, and functional deficit warrants surgery. Operative choices must preserve the physeal mechanism; ATFL/CFL repair or modified Broström-Gould with physeal-sparing are common, and internal bracing can augment primary repairs. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Pediatric chronic ligament reconstruction with modified Broström-Gould, with or without internal bracing, resolved pain and function and allowed return to sport while respecting growth plate anatomy</cite>.
- Technique considerations: Avoid deep lateral release or procedures that distract the distal tibia unless indicated; use medial or deep lateral physeal-sparing approaches and confirm syndesmotic congruency intraoperatively. Postoperatively, immediate protected motion with gradual loading, early isometric strengthening, and bracing/functional progression can be used to accelerate rehab while protecting the physeal union. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Respecting physeal anatomy enabled faster rehabilitation and return to activity after pediatric ligament reconstruction</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-3">postoperative care includes transition from splint/cast to CAM boot and then functional bracing with radiographic monitoring of mortise alignment</cite>.
- Alternatives and trade-offs: Syndesmotic fixation or more aggressive physeal closure may be required for high-grade syndesmotic injury, but in lateral ligament-only instability, growth-preserving techniques are preferred to minimize physeal arrest risk and maintain longitudinal growth. <cite id="3443e106-3">Pediatric syndesmotic injury management often includes brief immobilization and bracing with return to play guided by reduction maintenance and clinical course, reflecting growth-sensitive decision-making</cite>. 

Integrating skeletal maturity into rehabilitation and surgical planning
- Use skeletal age to individualize timelines and intensity: Growth plate status and maturity influence ligament healing, stability, and load tolerance. Early return to high-intensity cutting or valgus-inversion-heavy sports in an open physis increases physeal stress and recurrence risk; delaying sport exposure until near-closure may reduce growth-related complications but risks secondary tissue injury. <cite id="3443e106-2">Skeletal maturity strongly influences outcomes in pediatric ligament injury; premature return and activity intensity increase failure risk, and accurate maturity assessment helps time interventions and techniques to reduce growth disturbances and improve functional outcomes</cite>.

Use serial radiographs to confirm physeal alignment and rule out growth disturbances during recovery from syndesmotic or physeal-involving injuries. <cite id="3443e106-3">Functional bracing with early mobilization and radiographic surveillance are recommended to maintain mortise alignment during rehabilitation in pediatric syndesmotic injuries</cite>.
- Shared decision-making on “watch and grow”: In skeletally immature ankles with subjective instability but minimal mechanical laxity, nonoperative “wait to mature” with structured home-based neuromuscular and proprioceptive programs, activity modification, and annual clinical/readiometry review can be reasonable, reserving surgery for persistent symptoms and objective instability. <cite id="3443e106-3">There is variability and limited consensus in pediatric treatment algorithms, supporting individualized, watchful waiting with staged progression and referral to therapy</cite>.

Principles specific to open growth plates and skeletal immaturity

Surgical options in children must preserve the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and distal tibial physeal blood supply; modified Broström-Gould techniques with physeal-sparing are favored and allow accelerated rehab when used for persistent instability after failed conservative care. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Modified Broström-Gould with internal bracing in pediatric chronic lateral instability improved pain and function and enabled return to sport, contingent on respecting growth plate anatomy</cite>. 
- Emphasize neuromuscular and proprioceptive control: Pediatric programs should prioritize balance, coordination, and cut-down control due to higher recurrence risk and developmental instability perception. <cite id="3443e106-1">Chronic instability rehabilitation in pediatrics stresses continued physiotherapy with balance and proprioception</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-1">pediatric growth plate injury with concomitant ligament strain requires tailored rehab including neuromuscular and proprioceptive training to restore stability and facilitate safe return</cite>.

- Initial management and progression: PRICE early, then progressive weightbearing, range of motion, and strengthening with emphasis on functional control. Bracing or taping can enhance perceived stability but may not improve objective performance, so programs should not rely solely on supports; they should facilitate earlier mobilization with gradual return. <cite id="3443e106-1">Functional bracing with early mobilization outperforms immobilization for pediatric sprains, and bracing is recommended 3–6 months after return to activity and indefinitely with chronic instability, alongside proprioceptive training</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-3">functional braces that restrict external rotation (e.g., Malleoloc) are used after brief immobilization/casting and CAM booting, with serial radiographs to confirm mortise alignment and a tailored return-to-play protocol</cite>.

This pattern supports using braces conservatively in pediatrics to reduce recurrence perception while prioritizing neuromuscular and proprioceptive gains.
- Osteochondral protection in adolescents: High activity levels in juveniles increase microtrauma risk to the talus; rehab should include joint-protective loading, sport cessation during symptomatic spikes, and monitoring for osteochondral lesions. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-2">Adolescents frequently participate in organized sports, exposing ankles to repetitive microtrauma with relatively high incidence of juvenile osteochondral lesions; pediatric management aims to optimize outcomes across modalities</cite>.
- Treatment variability and the need for individualized plans: Pediatric lateral ankle injury management varies widely among clinicians, with inconsistent rationale between ankle vs syndesmotic injuries and between open vs closed physeas. This underscores the need for careful assessment and shared decision-making on immobilization duration, bracing, and referral to physical therapy. <cite id="3443e106-3">Surveyed pediatric orthopaedic practice shows variability in management of adult vs syndesmotic injuries in children, underrepresentation of low-energy lateral injuries in the literature, and that immobilization and therapy practices differ with limited evidence-based consensus</cite>.

Activity modification and return-to-sport in open physis
- Avoid high-valgus-inversion tasks initially: Restrict noncontact cutting, change-of-direction drills, and multidirectional jump-landing until ankle inversion range and knee valgus control normalize, and proprioception and strength are sport-specific. Teach toe-out/forefoot strike caution due to trade-offs in knee vs ankle risk. <cite id="018126a8-0">Lateral and diagonal landings pose greater recurrence risk than forward jumps for CAI athletes, implying targeted avoidance and retraining of these tasks</cite> and <cite id="e5e9a520-0">forefoot strategies can reduce knee valgus but may increase ankle inversion/inversion moment, so individualized technique training is required</cite>.
- Progressive exposure: Introduce cutting with a wide base, limited speed, closed chain, and high-tendon-cord plyometrics; reassess with validated instability-specific metrics (e.g., Star Excursion Balance Test, side hop, single-leg stance, perceived instability) before contact or multidirectional play. <cite id="018126a8-0">Multidirectional landings increase biomechanical risk and require enhanced rehab components to reduce recurrence</cite>.
- Duration of support and sport restrictions: Continue lace-up bracing or functional taping during high-risk sports or drills for 3–6 months postreturn to activity, and indefinitely if chronic instability persists; avoid bracing as a sole strategy and combine with control and strengthening. <cite id="3443e106-1">Bracing for 3–6 months after return to activity and indefinitely in persistent instability is recommended, with continued physiotherapy</cite>.
- Psychological readiness vs objective control: Because supports improve perceived stability without necessarily improving objective tests, integrate sport-specific drills that restore dynamic balance and coordination before full return, using perceived instability and drill performance as decision points. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-4">Ankle supports enhance self-reported and perceived stability but not objective functional test performance, so objective control should drive return decisions</cite>.

Surgical strategies when growth plates are open
- Indications and timing: Failed pediatric conservative care with persistent mechanical instability (positive drawer/translation), pain, and functional deficit warrants surgery. Operative choices must preserve the physeal mechanism; ATFL/CFL repair or modified Broström-Gould with physeal-sparing are common, and internal bracing can augment primary repairs. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Pediatric chronic ligament reconstruction with modified Broström-Gould, with or without internal bracing, resolved pain and function and allowed return to sport while respecting growth plate anatomy</cite>.

Postoperatively, immediate protected motion with gradual loading, early isometric strengthening, and bracing/functional progression can be used to accelerate rehab while protecting the physeal union. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-0">Respecting physeal anatomy enabled faster rehabilitation and return to activity after pediatric ligament reconstruction</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-3">postoperative care includes transition from splint/cast to CAM boot and then functional bracing with radiographic monitoring of mortise alignment</cite>.

Integrating skeletal maturity into rehabilitation and surgical planning
- Use skeletal age to individualize timelines and intensity: Growth plate status and maturity influence ligament healing, stability, and load tolerance. Early return to high-intensity cutting or valgus-inversion-heavy sports in an open physis increases physeal stress and recurrence risk; delaying sport exposure until near-closure may reduce growth-related complications but risks secondary tissue injury. <cite id="3443e106-2">Skeletal maturity strongly influences outcomes in pediatric ligament injury; premature return and activity intensity increase failure risk, and accurate maturity assessment helps time interventions and techniques to reduce growth disturbances and improve functional outcomes</cite>.
- Monitoring and readiness milestones: Track pain-free weightbearing, dorsiflexion and inversion-eversion control, single-leg balance (30–60 seconds), sport-specific hop symmetry (>90–95%), and validated instability questionnaires; allow gradual reintroduction to drills, then sport. Use serial radiographs to confirm physeal alignment and rule out growth disturbances during recovery from syndesmotic or physeal-involving injuries. <cite id="3443e106-3">Functional bracing with early mobilization and radiographic surveillance are recommended to maintain mortise alignment during rehabilitation in pediatric syndesmotic injuries</cite>.
- Shared decision-making on “watch and grow”: In skeletally immature ankles with subjective instability but minimal mechanical laxity, nonoperative “wait to mature” with structured home-based neuromuscular and proprioceptive programs, activity modification, and annual clinical/readiometry review can be reasonable, reserving surgery for persistent symptoms and objective instability. <cite id="3443e106-3">There is variability and limited consensus in pediatric treatment algorithms, supporting individualized, watchful waiting with staged progression and referral to therapy</cite>.

Putting it together: Pediatric ankle instability rehab with open growth plates
- Phase 1 (acute to early rehab, physeal protection): Early mobilization with protected motion, RICE, and functional bracing as tolerated; focus on gastrocnemius–soleus control, plantar flexor–dorsiflexor timing, and proprioception with balance over 6–12 weeks. Avoid cutting/landing and high-varus-valgus stress; use heel-toe walks, single-leg stance, closed-chain strengthening, and low-risk plyometrics. <cite id="3443e106-1">Functional bracing with early mobilization is more effective than immobilization for pediatric sprains, and bracing is recommended for 3–6 months after return to activity</cite> and <cite id="a0d2fb4d-1">pediatric injury programs should prioritize neuromuscular and proprioceptive training to restore stability</cite>.
- Phase 2 (functional restoration, sport-specific): Introduce midfoot and forefoot striking drills, deceleration and change of direction with wide bases, and low-speed lateral shuffles; reassess with instability measures. If multidirectional cutting is required, progress with taping/brace for the first 3–6 months and integrate neuromuscular drills that reduce knee valgus and ankle inversion moments. <cite id="018126a8-0">Lateral/diagonal landings pose higher recurrence risk and require enhanced rehab to prevent injury</cite> and <cite id="e5e9a520-0">forefoot vs rearfoot strategies trade off knee vs ankle risk factors, informing drill selection</cite>.
- Phase 3 (return to play and maintenance): Unbrace as stability permits; ensure hop symmetry, dynamic balance, and perceived instability are acceptable; allow gradual return with sport-specific contact and cutting, with ongoing monitoring for pain, swelling, and gait biomechanics. - Osteochondral and joint health: In adolescents, integrate joint-protective strategies—limit high-ankle valgus loads, avoid repetitive microtrauma during open physis, and consider imaging if clicking, swelling, or pain spikes occur; manage lesions with activity modification and targeted rehab before sport resumption. <cite id="a0d2fb4d-2">Adolescent sport participation elevates microtrauma risk for juvenile osteochondral lesions, necessitating careful management and outcome-focused rehab</cite>.

Title: Nonsurgical Rehabilitation Perspectives for a Type I Salter-Harris Fracture With Lipohemarthrosis and Concomitant Grade II Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Tear in a Volleyball Athlete: A Case Report
Snippet: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears represent common occurrences in sports, particularly posing significant risks to young athletes. The diagnostic methods for ACL injury include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), arthroscopy, and physical examination. Management of this injury can be done both operative and nonoperatively. Pediatric growth plate fractures are classified under the Salter-Harris classification. A 13-year-old male athlete sustained a knee injury during a volleyball match. While landing from a jump after a smash, the athlete directly landed on the ground on his right knee. After this, he reported discomfort and severe anterior knee pain. Due to immobility and pain, he was taken to the emergency unit. Upon radiographic examination, a Salter-Harris Classification Type I fracture was found, indicating epiphyseal slip and separation through the physis of the right proximal tibia medially. An MRI imaging was done to check the integrity of the ACL after the swelling had subsided post-15 days of injury. An MRI identified a bony contusion on the medial tibial plateau, extending to the physeal plate with a Grade II ACL tear. The concurrent occurrence of ACL injury and growth plate injury presents a significant concern. Hence, a referral for physical therapy rehabilitation was given. Where non-surgical rehabilitation strategies play a crucial role in managing these cases while focusing on restoring knee stability, promoting healing of the growth plate, and facilitating a safe return to sport. Tailored rehabilitation, including therapeutic exercises, neuromuscular training, and proprioceptive training, is essential for optimizing outcomes and preventing long-term complications. The case underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing the complex knee injury of this young athlete.

Title: Ankle supports enhance only psychological aspects of the Ankle-GO score in patients with chronic ankle instability.
Snippet: CONTEXT: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) is the most serious long-term complication following an ankle sprain. Taping and bracing are frequently employed in the return to sport (RTS) continuum to avoid injury recurrence and to maximize post-injury performance. The Ankle-GO score is a valid and reliable objective RTS criteria, but the influence of ankle supports on this score in CAI patients remains unknown.OBJECTIVES: We aimed to evaluate the induce effects of taping or bracing on the Ankle-GO score among patients suffering from CAI.DESIGN: Crossover StudySETTING: Sports medicine research laboratoryPATIENTS: Thirty CAI patients (13 males and 17 females, 33.4 ±11.7 years) performed the Ankle-GO score in three conditions (taping, bracing and no ankle support).MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The Ankle-GO is a 25-point score clustering 2 self-reported questionnaires (Foot and Ankle Ability Measure and Ankle Ligament Reconstruction-Return to Sport after Injury) and 4 functional tests (Single Leg Stance, Star Excursion Balance Test, Side Hop Test and Figure-of-eight test). Performances on each component as well as the total score were compared between conditions using repeated measures of ANOVA.RESULTS: Taping and bracing significantly and equally improved the Ankle-GO score compared with no support (12.8 ±5.3 and 11.2 ±4.2 vs. 8 ±4.5 points respectively, P<.001). However, significant improvements were found solely in self-reported questionnaires with ankle support (P<.001). No differences were found in functional tests, although both taping and bracing significantly lowered instability perception during the tests (+1.9 and +1.8 points, respectively).CONCLUSION: Ankle-GO scores were significantly enhanced with taping or bracing. However, only self-reported function and psychological readiness were improved. Functional performance was not altered, although external supports enhanced perceived stability. Both taping and bracing supports appear equally important in improving self-confidence and perceived ankle stability among individuals with CAI returning to sport.

Title: Skeletal Maturity Assessment in Pediatric ACL-Reconstruction
Snippet: Graft failure rates in pediatric patients are comparable to adults but are influenced by factors linked to skeletal maturity, such as premature return to sport and activity intensity [35]. Delaying surgery to avoid growth risks can increase secondary meniscal injuries, seen in up to 22% of conservatively managed cases [70]. Accurate maturity evaluation is therefore essential to balance timing and technique, reducing periods of instability that predispose to further injury. 

Complication patterns demonstrate the integral role of skeletal maturity assessment in pediatric ACLR. By guiding individualized timing and surgical strategy, precise maturity evaluation directly contributes to reducing growth disturbances and improving functional outcomes, addressing the core challenges highlighted by the research question.

snippet.text:
To address these gaps, this study investigated how forefoot and rearfoot landing strategies during stop-jumping maneuvers affect: (1) knee biomechanics related to ACL injury, (2) ankle biomechanics related to lateral ankle sprain risk, and (3) performance outcomes including jump height and stance time. 

Based on existing literature, we hypothesized that in recreational males, compared to rearfoot landing: (1) Forefoot landing would reduce ACL injury risk factors including peak knee valgus angle, knee extension moment, and anterior tibial shear force, (2) Forefoot landing would increase ankle injury risk factors including peak ankle inversion angle and inversion moment, and (3) Forefoot landing would enhance jump height and reduce stance time through more effective utilization of the stretch-shortening cycle.

Title: Sex difference in effect of ankle landing biomechanics in sagittal plane on knee valgus moment during single-leg landing
Snippet: Ankle landing strategies affects the biomechanical characteristics of the knee joint, especially knee frontal plane loading. However, no studies have investigated whether the association between ankle landing biomechanics in sagittal plane and the knee frontal plane loading differs between sexes. The purpose of this study was to examine whether there is a sex difference in the effect of ankle plantar flexion at the contact angle, ankle range of motion (ROM), and ankle plantar flexion moment on knee valgus loading during single-leg landing. Twenty-five females and twenty-four males performed a single-leg landing. Joint kinematics and kinetics of the lower extremities were measured. The relationship between ankle biomechanics in the sagittal plane (ankle plantar flexion angle at contact, ROM, and peak ankle plantar flexion moment) and peak knee valgus moment were analyzed. In males, the larger ankle plantarflexion angle at contact and ROM were significantly associated with lower peak knee valgus moment. In addition, in males only, a greater peak ankle plantar flexion moment was significantly associated with a lower peak knee valgus moment and greater peak ankle inversion moment. Altering ankle landing strategies in the sagittal plane during single-leg landing may reduce the knee valgus moment, which is one of risk factors for anterior cruciate ligament injury, in males only.
